title: Orionid Meteor Shower Peaks October 22: Best Time to Watch From India
excerpt: The Orionids peak before dawn on October 22 after moonset, with 10-20 meteors per hour under dark skies and a Mumbai window of about 3:30 to 5:15 a.m.
body:
• The Orionid meteor shower peaks on the night of October 21 into the morning of October 22; in India the best window is before dawn on October 22, after moonset.
  • In Mumbai that window is roughly 3:30 a.m. to 5:15 a.m. IST; expect about 10-20 meteors per hour under dark, moonless skies, and only a handful with moonlight.
  • No telescope is needed: pick a dark spot away from city lights, let your eyes adjust, and watch a broad stretch of sky rather than staring at Orion alone.
  • The meteors are debris from Halley's Comet, entering the atmosphere at about 66 km per second.

The Orionid meteor shower peaks this week, and India gets its best view in the pre-dawn hours of October 22, after the Moon sets and before the sky brightens. NASA's October skywatching guide, carried in full by WDRB/WAVE, puts the peak on the night of October 21 into the morning of October 22 and warns that a bright waxing gibbous Moon will wash out fainter meteors earlier in the night.

When to watch from India

Livemint's India viewing guide puts Mumbai's best window at roughly 3:30 a.m. to 5:15 a.m. IST on October 22, citing Stargazing Mumbai, with timings varying slightly by city. The radiant in Orion rises above the horizon around 10-11 p.m. in India and climbs through the night, passing almost overhead before dawn at latitudes similar to Mumbai's. Evening viewing is poor: the Orionids are a late-night shower, and moonlight makes the hours before moonset the least favourable.

Under dark, moonless conditions the peak produces about 10-20 meteors per hour. With moonlight present, viewers under typical rural skies may see only a handful, and sightings arrive in bursts, so quiet stretches are normal.

"When to watch from India Livemint's India viewing guide puts Mumbai's best window at roughly 3:30 a.m."

How to get the best view

Choose a safe, dark rural location away from bright city lights; a high-rise terrace is the city fallback. Settle into a reclining chair or sleeping bag and give your eyes time to adjust — NASA gives the same advice: find a dark location, let your eyes adapt, and look up. Before moonset, face east or northeast with the Moon behind you. After moonset, lie back and look overhead and towards the east, taking in as much open sky as possible.

Do not stare only at the radiant. The radiant lies in Orion's upper region near the reddish star Betelgeuse, close to the Orion-Gemini border, and Orion's three belt stars are the easiest way to find it. Meteors can streak across any part of the sky, and those farther from the radiant often leave the longest trails.

What you are actually seeing

The Orionids are dust and debris left behind by Halley's Comet. Earth passes through that debris stream every October, and particles enter the atmosphere at about 66 km per second, burning up as shooting stars. About half of Orionid meteors leave glowing trails that linger briefly. Halley last visited the inner solar system in 1986 and returns in 2061, so the annual shower is the closest most viewers will get to the comet itself.

For diaspora readers outside India, the same rule applies wherever you are: the peak night is October 21-22 local time, and the productive hours are after moonset and before dawn. One alarm, one dark spot and 30 unhurried minutes is the whole plan.
